transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Patel. What brings you in today?

I’m an EMT, and lately on emergency calls I feel like I’m moving wrong and doing the wrong things, like my actions don’t match what’s happening around me. My crew says I’m acting really off, and my supervisor ended up pulling me from duty and sending me here to get checked out.
Do you ever feel like you're watching yourself from outside your body or that the world around you feels unreal?

No, I don't feel like I'm watching myself from the outside or that the world around me isn't real. It's just that my own body feels out of sync with what's happening, and I can't seem to get myself to move the right way.
Do you feel disconnected from your own body or like you're not in control of your movements, even though you know it's your body moving?

Yes, it's like my body is on a completely different channel during calls. I'll find myself staring at my hands or doing something weirdly slow like carefully re-rolling bandages while everyone else is rushing around me. I know I'm off, but I just can't seem to snap into the right gear.
Have you ever had any seizures, head injuries, or episodes where you lost consciousness or awareness?
No, I've never had any seizures, head injuries, or episodes where I lost consciousness. Aside from feeling out of sync lately, my physical health has always been fine.
Do you ever feel like your body isn't yours, or that you're observing your movements from a distance, even if the world around you feels real?

No, I don't really feel like my body isn't mine or that I'm watching myself from a distance. It feels more like my body is just frozen or on a different channel and won't respond to what I want it to do, rather than me feeling detached from it.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidate was [F44], and based on this conversation, F44 remains the most consistent diagnosis. The patient describes a persistent sense of incoordination and lack of control over their movements during high-stress situations, specifically in the context of their work as an EMT, without depersonalization, derealization, or neurological symptoms such as seizures or loss of consciousness. The experience is not due to an external observer's perception alone, as the patient is aware of their abnormal movements and effort. There is no evidence of structural neurological disease or altered reality testing. The dissociative nature of the symptoms—focal disruption of motor control under stress, with preserved insight and absence of neurological findings—aligns with a dissociative motor disorder (ICD-10 code F44.4). No new symptoms suggest an alternative category such as psychosis, anxiety, or organic disorder, so the candidate list remains unchanged.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient experiences persistent subjective feelings of incoordination and lack of control over voluntary actions in the absence of neurological impairment, consistent with depersonalization-derealization disorder, specifically the depersonalization subtype. The disturbance is not better explained by another medical or psychiatric condition, and there is no evidence of delusions, hallucinations, or loss of consciousness.
